title: End-to-end encrypted sync
description: Sync where the server is blind: state encrypted client-side with keys the server never holds, synced as ciphertext. The server provides availability and ordering; confidentiality is entirely client-side. Signal's and Proton's sync work this way — the operator can't read what it stores.
method: Encrypt state with client keys; sync ciphertext; the server orders and stores blindly; clients decrypt locally.
usage: Keep keys off the server entirely; the server is untrusted storage, design accordingly.

demo.code:
print('state encrypted with device key; server stores ciphertext')
print('server breach: attacker gets noise (keys never present)')

title: Key rotation for shared state
description: Shared-state keys must rotate: members leave, devices are lost, and long-lived keys accumulate risk. Rotation re-encrypts state under a new key and distributes it to current members only — the departed member's key dies with their access. MLS (Messaging Layer Security) standardizes this for groups.
method: Generate new key; re-encrypt state; distribute to current members; revoke old; MLS for group messaging scale.
usage: Rotate on every membership change; schedule periodic rotation; automate it.

demo.code:
print('member leaves -> rotate: state re-encrypted under K2')
print('departed member holds K1: reads nothing new')

title: Sync integrity verification
description: A malicious server could fork the state (show different versions to different clients) or drop updates. Integrity verification — hash chains, Merkle trees over the log, gossip between clients — detects server misbehavior. CONIKS and Key Transparency do this for key directories; the same idea secures state sync.
method: Hash-chain the update log; clients gossip roots; mismatched roots expose forks; dropped updates break the chain.
usage: Gossip roots out-of-band periodically; treat mismatches as security incidents.

demo.code:
print('client A root: r7f2; client B root: r7f2 (gossip match)')
print('server fork attempt: roots diverge -> DETECTED')

title: Selective sync with encrypted filters
description: Devices don't need everything: selective sync downloads only matching state, with the server filtering on encrypted tags it can't read (via deterministic tag encryption or PIR). Bandwidth and exposure both drop — the phone syncs what it needs, blind to the server.
method: Tag state deterministically-encrypted; server filters on ciphertext tags; clients fetch matches; the server learns the filter pattern only.
usage: Use for large state on small devices; accept the filter-pattern leakage.

demo.code:
print('phone syncs: tag=enc("project-X") only (2% of state)')
print('server saw: a filter for some tag (which one: hidden)')

title: Offline-first secure sync
description: Offline-first means the local replica is primary: edits work without connectivity, sync merges when possible, and encryption never depends on the server being reachable. The security model holds offline — keys are local, ciphertext syncs when it can.
method: Local encrypted replica primary; sync opportunistically; merge on reconnect; keys never require the server.
usage: Design for offline from the start; test the merge-after-long-offline path.

demo.code:
print('offline 3 days: 42 local edits (encrypted at rest)')
print('reconnect: sync, merge, converge — no key ever needed the server')

title: Revocation propagation
description: When a device is lost or a member removed, revocation must propagate to every replica — including offline ones, which learn at next sync. The protocol marks the key dead, rotates, and quarantines data the revoked key touched after the compromise window.
method: Broadcast revocation; rotate keys; offline replicas learn on sync; quarantine post-compromise data for review.
usage: Automate revocation; assume offline devices exist; review quarantined data.

demo.code:
print('device lost -> revocation broadcast, keys rotated')
print('offline laptop syncs next week: learns revocation, re-encrypts')

title: Device pairing and provisioning
description: New devices join the sync mesh by pairing: an existing device verifies the new one (QR code, numeric comparison) and provisions the sync keys. Pairing is the trust root — a weak pairing flow lets attackers join the mesh and read everything.
method: Out-of-band verification (QR/numeric); provision keys over the verified channel; the new device syncs ciphertext after.
usage: Make pairing verification mandatory and unskippable; log new device joins.

demo.code:
print('new phone: scan QR from laptop (verified)')
print('keys provisioned; phone syncs ciphertext; join logged + notified')

title: Conflict resolution without decryption
description: When encrypted replicas conflict, the server (or the protocol) must order or merge without seeing content: deterministic timestamps, CRDT semantics on ciphertext, or client-side resolution after sync. The conflict logic operates on metadata and ciphertext structure, never plaintext.
method: Order by HLC timestamps; merge via encrypted-CRDT rules; clients resolve residual conflicts locally after decrypt.
usage: Design the conflict rules before the encryption; test concurrent encrypted edits.

demo.code:
print('concurrent edits: HLC orders them; CRDT merges ciphertext')
print('server resolved conflict having seen: timestamps only')
